planting.note: Plant dormant, nursery-propagated bare-root crowns in fall just below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained but evenly moist woodland soil in partial shade.

directions: Cypripedium 'Gisela' is a garden hybrid (C. macranthos x C. flavum parentage) bred to combine the vigor and adaptability of Asian lady's slipper species with showier flower color, producing rose-pink to magenta pouched blooms with a paler lip in late spring above pleated, ribbed foliage. It is considerably easier to establish and grow on than most wild-collected Cypripedium species, tolerating garden conditions better while still preferring a cool, humus-rich woodland bed with dappled shade and consistent moisture during the growing season. Mulch lightly with leaf litter each fall to protect the shallow root system and replicate its native forest-floor habitat, and avoid disturbing established clumps, which slowly bulk up into multi-stemmed specimens over years. Site alongside ferns and hostas in a shaded border where its unusual pouch flowers become a spring focal point.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer before they sprout, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs.

directions: Colchicum 'Waterlily' is a sterile double-flowered hybrid cultivar (a cross of C. autumnale and C. speciosum) prized for its large, many-petaled, rosy-lilac blooms that resemble a waterlily floating on bare soil, opening leafless in early autumn well before the coarse, strap-like foliage emerges the following spring. The heavy double flowers are more prone to flopping in rain than single colchicums, so siting under the light, dappled shade of deciduous trees or shrubs helps keep blooms cleaner and more upright than a fully exposed bed. Because the broad spring foliage persists for months and looks untidy as it yellows, interplant with later-emerging shade perennials such as hostas or ferns that will mask the dying leaves. All plant parts are toxic if ingested and should be planted away from grazing animals or edible garden beds.

planting.note: Plant divisions in aquatic containers set in 2-4 inches of standing water or saturated soil at a pond margin, in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani 'Zebrinus' is a sport of softstem bulrush selected for its leafless, rounded stems that are irregularly banded with horizontal cream-white and green stripes, giving the vertical, pencil-like foliage a distinctive candy-cane effect unlike any other pond-margin rush. Unlike full-sun wetland grasses, zebra rush holds its variegation and stays compact when given light afternoon shade in hot climates, making it useful for shaded water features and container water gardens where straight-species bulrushes would grow leggy. Divide congested clumps every 2-3 years in spring, discarding any all-green reverted stems promptly to keep the variegated pattern dominant in the clump. It spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a container when used in a lined pond to prevent it from colonizing the entire margin.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist to occasionally boggy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Juncus patens 'Elk Blue' is a selection of the Pacific Coast native gray rush chosen for its especially strong steel-blue foliage color, forming tight, upright, evergreen tufts of narrow round stems that hold their color better than the straight species through summer heat. It tolerates both boggy, saturated soil at a pond edge and ordinary garden moisture once established, and unlike many wetland rushes it also handles brief dry spells, making it a flexible choice for rain gardens or the damp partial shade beneath open-canopy trees. Its stiff, architectural, blue-gray vertical form provides useful textural and color contrast against broad-leaved shade perennials such as hostas and heucheras. Cut back hard in late winter every few years to remove old, browning stems and rejuvenate the clump.
